screens.body:
Usability testing is watching REAL users try your design — and it's the moment of truth for everything in this course. You give them tasks, they think aloud, and you watch where they stumble.

The golden rule: you're testing the DESIGN, not the user. If they can't find the button, the button is wrong — they are never wrong. Say it out loud at the start; it frees people to be honest.

options: Watching real users try the design — testing the design, never the user
Testing whether users are smart enough
check.question: Usability testing is…

screens.heading: The moment of truth
screens.keyPoint: Test the design, never the user.

screens.body:
Plan before you test: pick 3–5 realistic tasks ("book a braid appointment for Saturday"), recruit people who resemble real users, and write a short script — intro, tasks, debrief questions. Keep sessions to about 30–45 minutes.

Here's the famous finding: 5 users uncover most major problems. After five, you mostly hear repeats. So test with five, fix, then test with five more — instead of twenty once.

options: Realistic tasks, representative users, a short script — about 5 users per round
As many users as possible in one giant session
check.question: Planning a usability test:

screens.heading: Plan the session

screens.body:
During the session, your job is to observe — not help. Ask them to think aloud ("tell me what you're looking at"). When they struggle, resist the rescue instinct: the struggle IS the data.

Stay neutral: "mm-hmm" and "interesting" — never "no wait, click there!" Thank them warmly at the end regardless of how it went. A participant who felt judged won't be honest next time.

options: Observe neutrally, think-aloud, never rescue — the struggle is the data
Guide them to the right answers
check.question: Running the session:

screens.heading: Watch, don't rescue

screens.body:
Watch for four measures. Task success: did they complete it, yes or no? Time on task: how long did it take? Errors: wrong turns, misclicks, backtracking. Satisfaction: how did it FEEL — ask them after, simply.

Numbers don't replace watching, but they let you compare rounds: "success went from 40% to 90% after the redesign" is how you prove the iteration worked.
screens.heading: What to measure

screens.body:
One user stumbling might be a fluke; three users stumbling at the same spot is a finding. Look for PATTERNS across sessions, then rate each problem's severity: cosmetic (annoying), minor (slows down), major (blocks the task), catastrophic (data loss, can't recover).

Severity decides what gets fixed first. A catastrophic bug found by one user outranks a cosmetic gripe found by five — impact beats frequency.

options: Patterns across users, rated by severity (cosmetic → catastrophic)
check.question: Finding the real problems:

screens.heading: Patterns, then severity

screens.body:
Findings become fixes, prioritized by severity — then you redesign and TEST AGAIN. That retest is non-negotiable: it's how you confirm the fix worked and didn't break something else.

This is the iteration loop closing: research → design → test → fix → test. Each loop should make the numbers move. If success rates aren't climbing, the redesign missed the real cause — dig deeper, not prettier.

options: Prioritize by severity, redesign, and retest to confirm
Fix everything at once without retesting
check.question: From findings to fixes:

screens.heading: Fix, then prove it
screens.keyPoint: Retest — that's how you know the fix worked.

screens.body:
Wrap up by recommending improvements clearly: what worked well (protect it), what fell short (with evidence — "4 of 5 users missed the submit button"), and the concrete next steps, ordered by priority.

Good recommendations are specific and doable: "move the submit button above the fold and retest" beats "improve the form." Stakeholders fund specific; they shelve vague.

options: What worked, what fell short (with evidence), and specific prioritized next steps
check.question: Recommending improvements means…

screens.heading: Report like a pro

screens.body: Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — the definitive guides on running usability tests and think-aloud protocol. Usability.gov — free U.S. government templates for test plans and reporting. W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (w3.org/WAI) — include users with disabilities in your testing.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: NNG's test guides are the industry playbook.
